description:
Hyunim Baek - majoring horticulture 
Kiwan Jeon - Data science & Statistics

Jun-Sang Kim - Software Engineering
summary: Field Shift is a free web tool that helps farmers choose crop rotations for the climate their field has now, not the one it had 30 years ago. A farmer drops a pin on their field. Field Shift pulls 44 years of daily NASA POWER weather for that exact point and shows, in plain words, how the season has shifted since 1981–2000: frost dates, heat, rainfall, dry spells and water demand. It adds the field's soil (USDA SSURGO or SoilGrids) and a crop knowledge base in which every value is cited. It then generates every rotation that follows basic farming rules and ranks them against the farmer's current practice, using the priorities the farmer ranks: soil health, water, yield stability and simplicity. Each recommendation explains why, tied to a measured change. Near Ames, Iowa, for example, the first fall frost now comes 9 days later, which leaves room for a cereal rye cover crop after harvest. Farmers face shifting seasons, tighter water and declining soil health, but rarely get field-level evidence of how their own conditions changed. Field Shift gives them that evidence, and rotation options they can explore.
details:
What it does. Field Shift turns NASA Earth-observation data into a field-level crop rotation decision. For any point on Earth it:

  1. Compares 1981–2000 with 2005–2024 at that exact point: growing degree days, days above 35 °C, growing-season rain and its variability, the longest dry spell, reference evapotranspiration (ET0), root-zone soil wetness and frost dates. Where there is no regular frost, it measures the start, end and length of the rainy season instead. Each change comes with a one-line meaning for a farmer.
  2. Detects the soil: USDA SSURGO in the US (texture, water-holding capacity, organic matter, drainage) or ISRIC SoilGrids elsewhere. The farmer can override it with a soil texture.
  3. Asks what the farmer grows now, and has them rank four priorities (soil health, water conservation, yield stability, simplicity) instead of typing numbers. Any priority can be marked “doesn’t matter”.
  4. Generates every 2–5 year rotation from a regional crop pack and filters it with farming rules: no annual crop two years in a row, alfalfa stands of 2–3 years, winter wheat only after an early enough harvest, no alfalfa on poorly drained soil. Where the harvest leaves enough days before the site’s current first fall frost, it adds a cover crop.
  5. Simulates each crop through 20 seasons of real daily weather with an FAO-56 root-zone water balance, and scores irrigation gap, FAO-33 water-limited yield loss, mid-season heat days, fertilizer nitrogen after legume credits, soil cover, crop and family diversity, and simplicity.
  6. Ranks the rotations against the farmer’s current practice and explains each one in plain language. The farmer can swap any crop and re-score instantly. A methodology panel shows every formula, input and source.

How it works. A Python FastAPI backend calls the NASA POWER and EONET APIs, USDA Soil Data Access and SoilGrids, caches every response, and computes FAO-56 Penman-Monteith ET0 from POWER weather. Every value in the crop knowledge base cites a source (177 values from 19 sources); a value without a source stays empty and the measure that needs it is skipped, never guessed. The Next.js website uses Leaflet for the map and Recharts for charts. Priority ranks become weights with the rank-order centroid method (Barron & Barrett 1996). Two demo fields (Ames, Iowa and Niamey, Niger) are saved as snapshots, so the demo also runs offline.

Example. Near Ames, the frost-free season grew from 168 to 179 days, but the air now demands 46 mm more water a year and growing-season rain fell 41 mm. Against continuous corn (score 22.9 with soil health ranked first), the top rotation is three years of alfalfa then corn with cereal rye (71.6): fertilizer nitrogen falls from 203 to 28 kg/ha a year and soil cover rises from 73% to 94% of the year. Rank simplicity first and plain corn–soybean becomes the top pick. Near Niamey, Niger, the tool tracks the rainy season instead (10 days longer, but with longer dry breaks) and suggests adding legumes to pearl millet.

Benefits and intended impact. Field-level, explainable evidence instead of a black box: every recommendation is tied to a measured local shift, and every number can be traced to its source. It works anywhere NASA POWER and SoilGrids have data, and runs in a browser with no account or install. We hope it starts better conversations between farmers and agronomists about adapting rotations to a changing climate.

What makes it creative. Rotations are generated from rules for each field instead of picked from a fixed list, the climate shift drives the explanation (“frost now comes 9 days later, so rye fits”), and farmers rank priorities in plain terms and can swap crops to explore their own ideas.

Factors we considered. Honest indicators (scores are relative, not yield predictions), farmer-friendly language, global coverage with richer US data, and reliability (cached data and an offline demo mode). Limitations: crop data is richest for the US Midwest; some tropical crop values are not sourced yet; regions with two rainy seasons a year are not handled well yet; irrigated farming is not modelled.

Tools. Python 3.12, FastAPI, pandas, NumPy, pytest (73 tests); TypeScript, Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, Recharts; hosted on Vercel (website) and Render (API). Code: https://github.com/jszz27/field-shift (MIT license).
dataRefs: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources) daily point API, AG community: T2M, T2M_MAX, T2M_MIN, PRECTOTCORR, RH2M, WS2M, ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN, GWETTOP, GWETROOT, 1981-2024
NASA EONET (Earth Observatory Natural Event Tracker) v3: drought, flood, storm, temperature-extreme and wildfire events (context only)
projectRefs: USDA NRCS SSURGO soil survey (Soil Data Access)
FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56: crop evapotranspiration (ET0, crop coefficients, rooting depth)
FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 66 / 33: crop yield response to water (Ky)
Sacks et al. (2010) SAGE Crop Calendar Dataset (Southern Hemisphere planting dates)
USDA NASS Agricultural Handbook 628: usual planting and harvesting dates (2010)
Iowa State University (Sawyer 2008): corn nitrogen rates after soybean and corn
K-State Research and Extension MF2586: nitrogen recommendations and credits
University of Minnesota Extension: alfalfa establishment (soil and drainage)
SARE, Cover Crops (Myers), Ch. 6: cover crop timing
USDA Technical Bulletin 1935 (2013): crop temperature thresholds
Full list of crop-value sources (crops.json, in the app under "How each score is computed")
Natural Earth country outlines via world-atlas (offline map)
Anthropic Claude (Claude Code): AI coding and writing assistant, see README "Use of AI"
No Space Agency Partner data was used
